clue.text: Prove right, merely by changing book to Kipling poem

indicators.note: the instruction says one letter standing for a volume is swapped out and a poem title put in its place

parts.note: merely means only, just
taken as written
B is the abbreviation for book
If— is Rudyard Kipling's best-known poem

explanation.surface: An editor vindicates a choice by swapping a book in an anthology for a Kipling poem.
explanation.walkthrough: JUST BY becomes JUSTIFY once the B is replaced with IF.
explanation.definitionFit: To justify an action is to show that it was correct or reasonable, vindicating it.

clue.text: Two little women with start of lock jaw

parts.note: Jo is one of Alcott's Little Women, and W is the little, abbreviated, form of women

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of lock

explanation.surface: Two small girls, one with the beginning of a lock of hair against a jaw.
explanation.walkthrough: The two women are given two different ways: Jo, the March sister in Little Women, and W, the standard abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A jowl is the lower part of the cheek and jaw, especially when fleshy or sagging.

clue.text: The lead for which one was unprepared?

definitions.text: The lead for which one was unprepared?

parts.words: The lead for which one was unprepared?
parts.note: surface reading: an actor or detective given a lead role or clue without warning
setter's reading: lead is the metal Pb, a chemical element, and this one caught you off guard

explanation.walkthrough: Lead looks like a leading role or a clue to follow; read as the metal, it is a chemical element, and an unexpected one is the phrase for a sudden advantage.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means the advantage of catching an opponent off guard, punned here as an unexpected chemical substance.

clue.text: Badly behind, missing third payment, ultimately still owing

indicators.note: something done badly is botched and jumbled, so the letters come out in a new order
missing means lacking, and third points at the letter in third position of the word before it

parts.note: taken as written; its third letter H is dropped

indicators.note: ultimately means at the very end, so the final letter is taken

parts.note: the final letter of payment

explanation.surface: Someone badly behind with payments, having missed the third instalment, still owes money.
explanation.walkthrough: BEHIND loses its H to become BEIND, then T is added and the six letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in debt is to owe money that has not yet been repaid to a creditor.

clue.text: Young professional lady's ending up tart?

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its last letter, which is all that is kept

parts.note: the last letter of lady
taken as written
a tart is a kind of pie

explanation.surface: Asks whether a young career woman will end up as a tart, a loose woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Tart looks like an insult for a woman; here it is pastry. The 's reads as 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Yuppie is the 1980s coinage for a young urban professional with a well-paid job and expensive tastes.

clue.text: One disposing of irritations following Labour Party round

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
L is the abbreviation for Labour, the UK political party

indicators.note: turned round means facing the other way, so the word runs right to left

parts.note: taken as written, then turned round

explanation.surface: A Labour politician disposes of irritating colleagues after a round of party meetings.
explanation.walkthrough: The irritations are flies, and a flytrap, the plant or the device, gets rid of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A flytrap catches and kills flies, which are the small pests or annoyances described cryptically.

clue.text: In terror, disorderly go to pumps?

indicators.note: disorderly means out of order, so the letters following are scrambled
in places the jumbled letters inside the word for dread

parts.note: terror is great fear
the letters of go to rearranged

explanation.surface: Terrified people flee in disorder towards the pumps, as if from a fire.
explanation.walkthrough: Pumps looks like machinery; it is light shoes, an example of the definition, hence the question mark. A pump is a plain shoe or a plimsoll in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Footgear covers all shoes and boots, and pumps are one example of such footwear.

clue.text: Volunteers of yore, with many suffering

indicators.note: suffering words are knocked about and put out of shape, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Volunteer soldiers of olden days, many of them enduring hardship.
explanation.walkthrough: The British Yeomanry were volunteer cavalry regiments, originally raised from small landowners.
explanation.definitionFit: The yeomanry was a volunteer mounted force in Britain, so its members are collectively volunteers.

clue.text: Chambers won't have an entry here, if you're lucky!

definitions.text: Chambers won't have an entry here, if you're lucky!

parts.words: Chambers won't have an entry here
parts.note: surface reading: the Chambers dictionary lacks a headword for some term
setter's reading: the chambers of a revolver, and the entry is a bullet; if luck holds, the one that fires is empty

explanation.walkthrough: Chambers is the famous dictionary used by crossword setters, so an entry sounds like a headword; it is the cylinder of a gun with one live round.
explanation.definitionFit: In this deadly game a player spins a revolver loaded with a single bullet and fires at their own head.

clue.text: One retiring medic follows another back into queue behind Dad — or Mum, for example

indicators.note: follows fixes the order: the first-named doctor comes after the second

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father

indicators.note: going back into somewhere means being put inside it, here inside the word for a queue

parts.note: a queue is a line of people

indicators.note: behind sets the queue after the father in the word

parts.note: another medic: DR, short for doctor

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing backwards, so that doctor's title is read in the other direction

parts.note: MO, the Medical Officer, a military doctor; this one is turned round

explanation.surface: A queue of patients behind a father, one doctor retiring and another following, with a mention of mum.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes Mum look like an alternative to Dad; it is the definition by example. MO is the Medical Officer, an army doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: Mum reads the same forwards and backwards, so it is an example of a word that is symmetrical in spelling.

clue.text: Express boarded by Latin Society

indicators.note: something boarded by a passenger has that passenger inside it

parts.note: to express is to put into words, to word
L is the abbreviation for Latin

explanation.surface: A Latin Society boards an express train.
explanation.walkthrough: Express looks like a train, which makes boarded natural; it is the verb meaning to phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The world can mean human society at large, as in the world of fashion or the wider world.

clue.text: Magistrate's conflicting votes left America in recession

parts.note: votes for and against: pro and con

indicators.note: a recession is a going back, so those letters are read backwards

parts.note: L for left
US for the United States

explanation.surface: A magistrate's split vote has left America in an economic recession.
explanation.walkthrough: Recession looks economic; it means retreating. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A proconsul was a Roman official, a governor with judicial powers in a province, so a kind of magistrate.

clue.text: Big, big band in organ rendition

indicators.note: a rendition is a fresh performance or version, so the letters before it are played in a new order

parts.note: all fourteen letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A big band's arrangement is played on an organ.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'Big' is the definition; the second is part of the letters to be mixed.
explanation.definitionFit: Brobdingnag is the land of giants in Gulliver's Travels, so its adjective means huge or gigantic.

clue.text: Commercial transport showing considerable stress

parts.note: as in a good few or a good deal: considerable
strain is stress or tension

explanation.surface: Commercial transport is under considerable stress, as in a struggling haulage industry.
explanation.definitionFit: A goods train carries freight rather than passengers, making it transport for trade and business.

clue.text: Serviceable fellow rejected northern banker

indicators.note: something rejected is thrown out, so that letter is removed

parts.note: serviceable means of use
F is the abbreviation for fellow

explanation.surface: A useful colleague turned down by a bank in the north of England.
explanation.walkthrough: Banker is crossword shorthand for a river, which has banks; the Ouse flows through York.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ouse is a river in Yorkshire, northern England, and any river has banks on either side.

clue.text: War and Peace personified: not I — the king's old gamekeeper

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: not here means without, so the letter that follows is taken out

parts.note: Irene, or Eirene, is the Greek goddess who personifies peace
taken as written
R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A literary puzzle about Tolstoy's novel and an old royal gamekeeper.
explanation.walkthrough: War and Peace looks like the Tolstoy title; it is WAR plus the goddess Irene, who loses her I.
explanation.definitionFit: A warrener was historically the keeper of a rabbit warren on an estate, a kind of gamekeeper.

clue.text: Number 50 secures bye to last place in quarter-final — my pleasure!

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast inside, so the farewell sits within

parts.note: No. is the abbreviation for number
L is fifty in Roman numerals
ta-ta is an informal goodbye, so bye

indicators.note: the last place in a word is its final letter, which alone is kept

parts.note: the final letter of quarter-final

explanation.surface: A tennis seed numbered fifty wins a bye into the quarter-final.
explanation.walkthrough: Bye looks like the sporting free pass; it is a farewell. Ta-ta is a chiefly British way of saying goodbye.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are polite replies to thanks, waving the favour away as no trouble.

clue.text: Like a fool, puts up with way layabout behaves

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means reading from the bottom upwards, so backwards

parts.note: taken as written, then turned upwards
a layabout behaves lazily, doing nothing

explanation.surface: A fool puts up with how a layabout behaves.
explanation.walkthrough: Puts up with looks like one phrase meaning tolerates; it splits into the reversal and a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting stupidly means acting foolishly, without sense, as a fool would.

clue.text: Round the twist or up the pole?

indicators.note: twisting something bends it out of shape, so the letters around it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Asks whether someone is round the twist or up the pole: two British ways of saying mad.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'round the twist' and 'up the pole' are British slang for crazy, so the clue looks like a pair of synonyms.
explanation.definitionFit: Heading straight towards the North Pole is travelling directly north on the compass.

clue.text: The Animals may initially make a persistent noise!

parts.note: a zoo is a collection of animals

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so just the first letter is used

parts.note: the first letter of may

explanation.surface: The 1960s rock group The Animals may make a lot of noise.
explanation.walkthrough: The Animals were a British band, which makes noise seem musical.
explanation.definitionFit: To zoom is to make a continuous low humming or buzzing sound, as a fast engine does.

clue.text: That is a horse beetle

parts.note: sc., short for Latin scilicet, means that is to say
an Arab is a breed of horse

explanation.surface: Points at an insect and names it a horse beetle.
explanation.walkthrough: SC is less common than i.e. for 'that is', but setters use it.
explanation.definitionFit: The scarab is a dung beetle, sacred in ancient Egypt and often carved as an amulet.

clue.text: Show fear — this is a case for Robin Hood

definitions.meaning: first meaning: tremble, shake with fright
second meaning: the container for an archer's arrows

explanation.walkthrough: Case for Robin Hood sounds like a legal case; it is something holding arrows.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for trembling with emotion and a noun for an archer's arrow holder.

clue.text: Besotted, they pop without introduction up chapel!

definitions.text: Besotted, they pop without introduction up chapel

indicators.note: besotted means befuddled, as if drunk, so the letters are muddled
without its introduction a word loses its first letter

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, then losing its first letter
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A smitten pair pop up to the chapel to get married.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue both supplies the letters and describes the newlyweds heading to their wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the usual name for a bride and groom, two besotted people who wed in a chapel.

clue.text: Adverse criticism almost to the end of the scale

indicators.note: going almost to the end stops short by one, so the last letter is left off

parts.note: a scale is a thin flake, as of skin

explanation.surface: Criticism that runs almost to the top of the scale.
explanation.walkthrough: Scale looks like a range of measurement; it is a small flake.
explanation.definitionFit: Flak, originally anti-aircraft fire, is used figuratively for strong hostile criticism or opposition.

clue.text: Great conqueror's kiss collected by a beautiful youth

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something collected by another is gathered up and held inside it

parts.note: Leander, lover of Hero in Greek myth, was a handsome young man
X is the conventional written kiss

explanation.surface: A conqueror steals a kiss from a handsome young man.
explanation.walkthrough: Leander swam the Hellespont nightly to visit Hero. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander the Great of Macedon conquered an empire stretching from Greece to India.

clue.text: Essential part finally bottled?

indicators.note: something bottled is put inside a small glass vessel

parts.note: a vial is a small bottle, which holds the letter

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so the last letter is taken

parts.note: the final letter of part

explanation.surface: Asks whether the essential element was finally bottled.
explanation.walkthrough: Bottled does double duty: it signals the insertion and supplies the bottle itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Something vital is absolutely necessary or indispensable to life or success.

clue.text: Clear drama enacted on court?

parts.note: to clear a sum after costs is to net it
a play is a drama

explanation.surface: A clear-cut piece of drama acted out in a courtroom.
explanation.walkthrough: Court looks legal; it is a tennis court, where net play is volleying close to the net.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis, play at the net means volleys and smashes performed on the court near it.

clue.text: Fool's eating bitter plant off the wall!

indicators.note: something eating another takes it inside itself

parts.note: berk is British slang for a fool
ers is the bitter vetch, a plant name setters favour

explanation.surface: A fool eats a bitter plant and goes wild.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is'. ERS goes inside BERK after its B.
explanation.definitionFit: Going berserk means becoming wildly out of control, as does behaviour that is crazy or bizarre.
